title: Forensic foundations
description: The foundations every forensic examination rests on: the scientific principles of digital forensics, the kinds of digital evidence, collecting in order of volatility, the Indian legal framework for electronic evidence, chain of custody, documentation, professional ethics and building a safe forensic lab.

lessons.title: Forensic principles
lessons.summary: What digital forensics is, the seven working principles that make findings defensible, and how examination works as hypothesis testing on verified copies.
objectives: Define digital forensics and explain what forensic evidence can and cannot answer
Apply the seven working principles to decisions on a live incident
Explain the integrity model linking the original, image, working copy and findings
Test competing hypotheses by seeking observations that could rule each out
Label statements in a report as fact, inference or opinion

lessons.title: Evidence types
lessons.summary: How to classify digital evidence by source, stability, provenance and origin of content, and what each classification means for handling, integrity claims and corroboration, using a fictional intake receipt and the course acquisition transcript.
objectives: Classify evidence items by source, form and stability, provenance and origin of content
Identify the integrity anchor of an item and state what a hash at that point does and does not establish
Review an intake receipt for missing provenance, scope boundaries and time-basis gaps
Interpret the course acquisition transcript as a record of an original, a forensic copy, a working copy and a changed copy
Distinguish independent corroborating sources from multiple copies of a single source

lessons.title: Order of volatility
lessons.summary: How the RFC 3227 order of volatility ranks evidence by expected lifetime, what to avoid at a running system, and what each way of stopping or keeping a machine running preserves and loses.
objectives: Explain the forces that shorten evidence lifetime and rank sources with the RFC 3227 order
Adapt the order to the real log rotation and retention of a given system
Identify the actions RFC 3227 warns against and the evidence each destroys
Record a system's clock offset against a UTC reference
Choose between keeping a machine running, capturing memory and shutting down, and record what is given up

lessons.title: Legal handling in India
lessons.summary: The Indian legal framework for electronic evidence from a practitioner's view: the BSA and its Section 63 certificate, BNSS search and seizure, IT Act examiners, CERT-In directions and personal data.
objectives: Identify the laws that apply to electronic evidence in India and when the BSA and BNSS came into force
Explain what the BSA Section 63 certificate asks for and which lab records support it
Describe BNSS requirements for recording search and seizure and for forensic experts at the scene
Relate CERT-In log retention and clock synchronisation directions to forensic readiness
Apply data minimisation and recognise which decisions belong to counsel and the court

lessons.title: Chain of custody
lessons.summary: How a chronological, signed record of every holder, location, transfer and seal state shows that an evidence item and its derived copies are what they claim to be.
objectives: Explain how continuity and integrity differ and how hashes and custody records support each
Complete an evidence receipt and custody log entry that answer who, what, when, where, why and how
Distinguish physical items from derived items and start a custody record for an image or export
Review a custody log for broken links, seal discrepancies and time-zone errors
Correct and document custody gaps without altering earlier records

lessons.title: Documentation
lessons.summary: How contemporaneous notes, examination and decision logs and a structured case file make forensic work reproducible, reviewable and accountable.
objectives: Describe the record types in a case file and the reviewer question each answers
Write timed, specific contemporaneous notes that keep observation, inference and opinion separate
Record tool versions, outputs, failures and decisions not to examine with reasons
Rewrite weak notes into reviewable notes and document a peer review
Apply access, integrity and minimisation controls to a case file

lessons.title: Ethics
lessons.summary: The professional duties that keep privileged forensic access tied to its purpose: scope and restraint, objectivity, honest correction of errors, accurate tool and certainty claims, competence, independence and confidentiality.
objectives: Apply a scope-first decision to items met during authorised work, treating uncertainty as out of scope and logging the outcome
Distinguish observations, inferences and opinions, and report material that weakens the requester's theory
Respond openly to an altered working copy or a mistyped digest using the saved C09 acquisition transcript
Rewrite overclaiming statements about tools, integrity and attribution into defensible, evidence-tied wording
Identify conflicts of interest, competence limits and confidentiality duties in realistic case scenarios

lessons.title: Lab setup
lessons.summary: Build an isolated, inventoried and organised analysis workstation, then prove its verification routine with the original C09 acquisition transcript and offline file-based checks on synthetic data.
objectives: Design a case folder layout in which evidence moves one way from intake receipt to verified working copy
Configure an isolated analysis VM with UTC time, a tool inventory and a recorded clean-baseline snapshot
Interpret each step of the original C09 acquisition transcript as a check on the lab's own verification routine
Demonstrate with a manifest check that the routine reports a match on unchanged files and a failure on changed files
Distinguish a local known-answer check from formal tool testing and from any guarantee of legal admissibility
